unit1_notes.pdf: 1 UNIT 1 — THE CONNECTED WORLD Communication, Networks & Computing 1.1 COMPUTER NETWORKS & THE INTERNET Communication and telecommunications (Slides 3 – 7) Every communication system can be understood through five elements: sender, message, medium or channel, receiver, and an agreed method of interpretation. For example, when a student sends a voice note, the microphone converts sound into electrical signals, the phone represents the sound as digital data, the network carries the data, and the receiving phone reconstructs audible sound. Noise, weak signals and congestion may reduce communication quality. Feedback, such as a reply or delivery confirmation, tells the sender whether the message was received. Telecommunication means communicating over a distance us ing a technical medium. The telegraph transmitted coded electrical signals; the telephone made two - way voice communication practical; radio enabled wireless broadcasting; and television combined sound and moving pictures. Modern digital communication repre sents information as bits (0s and 1s). This common digital representation makes it possible for the same network to carry text, voice, images, video and sensor readings. Consider a video call: the camera and microphone capture information, software compres ses it, packets travel through several networks, and the other device decodes and displays the result. This example shows why communication, computing and networking are closely related. Communication means transferring information from a source to a desti nation through a channel. The message may be speech, text, image, video or digital data. For successful communication, the sender and receiver must agree on how information is represented and interpreted. Telecommunications extends communication over dista nce. Earlier methods such as messengers and written letters evolved into telegraph, telephone, radio, television and digital communication. Modern networks carry many types of information over shared infrastructure. Networks, internetworking and the Intern et (Slides 8 – 10) A network is more than a set of computers placed near each other. Devices must have network interfaces, a communication medium, suitable addressing and common rules. In a college laboratory, computers may connect to a switch using Ethernet cables; the switch enables communication within the local area network (LAN). A router then connects this LAN to another network or to the Internet. Internetworking is the process of linking different networks so that information can cross network boundar ies. The Internet is a global internetwork, not a single centrally owned network. It contains

2 home networks, university networks, mobile networks, service - provider networks and data - center networks. Internet Protocol (IP) helps packets move between these d iverse systems. The Internet of People describes the use of connectivity for human activities such as email, social media and video meetings. The Internet of Things extends this idea to sensors, machines, vehicles and appliances that exchange data and may take action automatically. The underlying goal remains the same: useful information must move between connected endpoints. A computer network is a group of interconnected devices that can exchange information and share resources. A local network may connec t laboratory computers and printers. Internetworking joins multiple independent networks using devices such as routers. The Internet is the worldwide system of interconnected networks that communicate using the TCP/IP protocol suite. The “Internet of Peopl e” emphasizes human communication through messaging, websites and social platforms; the Internet of Things extends connectivity to physical objects. Why networking needs common rules (Slides 11 – 17) The air - transport analogy in the slides helps explain the scale of the problem. An airline cannot operate safely using only an aircraft: it also needs airports, flight routes, identification, air - traffic control and shared procedures. Similarly, a computer cannot communicate across the world using only a cable. N etwork interfaces, switches, routers, addressing systems, routing mechanisms and protocols must cooperate. A protocol is a documented set of communication rules. It defines matters such as the format of a message, the order in which messages are exchanged, how a receiver identifies the sender, and what happens if an error occurs. Imagine two people speaking different languages without translation: both can produce sounds, but meaningful communication fails. Protocols provide the shared language for digital systems. Layering divides a complex networking task into smaller functions. One layer handles application requirements, another reliable transfer, another routing, and another local transmission. A layer can change its internal technology while still offer ing the same service to the layer above. This separation simplifies design, standardization and troubleshooting. Early computers were often isolated and used incompatible hardware, operating systems and communication technologies. The presentation compares networking with an air - transport system: airports, pilots, air - traffic control, routes and regulations must coordinate to move passengers safely. Similarly, computer networks need addressing, routes, equipment and rules to move data. A protocol is an agre ed set of rules specifying how data is formatted, transmitted, received and acknowledged. Dividing networking into layers makes a large task manageable: each layer has a responsibility and offers services to the layer above it.

3 OSI reference model: seven l ayers (Slides 18 – 20) The OSI model has seven layers. Layer 7, Application, supports network - facing functions used by software, such as web access and email. Layer 6, Presentation, deals conceptually with representation of information, including character e ncoding and data transformation. Layer 5, Session, concerns establishing and managing exchanges between applications. These three upper layers describe functions that practical Internet protocols may combine. Layer 4, Transport, provides communication betw een application processes on different hosts. Layer 3, Network, determines logical addresses and routes packets between networks. Layer 2, Data Link, organizes bits into frames for delivery across a local link and uses local addressing such as MAC addresse s. Layer 1, Physical, transmits bits as electrical, optical or radio signals. When data is sent, it moves down the layers. Each relevant layer adds information needed for its work; this is called encapsulation. At the receiver, the corresponding headers ar e interpreted and removed as the message moves upward; this is decapsulation. An analogy is placing a letter inside an envelope, adding a delivery label, and transporting it through a delivery system. The OSI model is a learning and troubleshooting referen ce, not a claim that every network uses seven separate software modules. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) developed the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model to describe network communication in seven layers. Physical t ransmits bits as signals. Data Link transfers frames over a local link and handles local addressing and error detection. Network supports logical addressing and routing. Transport supports end - to - end communication and reliability where needed. Session orga nizes communication sessions. Presentation deals with representation, encoding and related transformations. Application provides network services to software. At the sender, data passes down the layers and each layer adds control information (encapsulation ). At the receiver, corresponding information is interpreted or removed (decapsulation). The OSI model is primarily a conceptual reference for understanding and troubleshooting. How TCP/IP emerged (Slides 21 – 27) As research networks expanded, computers bui lt by different organizations needed a common way to communicate. ARPANET research and the development of TCP and IP contributed to a protocol family that could connect dissimilar networks. TCP/IP became the practical basis of Internet communication becaus e it defined interoperable methods for addressing, routing and exchanging data. The four - layer TCP/IP model used in the presentation starts with the Application layer, where services such as web browsing and email operate. The Transport layer uses TCP or U DP to communicate between processes. The Internet layer uses IP to forward packets across networks. The Host - to - Network or Network Access layer handles transmission over the immediate wired or wireless network.

4 The OSI and TCP/IP models should not be confu sed. OSI has seven conceptual layers; TCP/IP commonly groups the top three OSI layers into one Application layer and the bottom two into Network Access. The names and exact boundaries may vary between textbooks. For this unit, remember the four - layer repre sentation shown in the slides. Different research and commercial networks needed a common way to exchange information. Work supported by ARPA/DARPA led to the TCP/IP protocol suite, which became the foundation of the Internet. Unlike the seven - layer OSI re ference model, the four - layer TCP/IP model used in these slides groups responsibilities into Application, Transport, Internet and Host - to - Network (Network Access). Application includes HTTP, DNS and email protocols; Transport includes TCP and UDP; Internet includes IP; and Host - to - Network includes technologies such as Ethernet and Wi - Fi. The two models describe similar functions with different groupings. TCP/IP is a working protocol suite rather than simply a theoretical diagram. IP addressing, packets and routing (Slides 28 – 30) An IP address is a logical network - layer address used to identify a network interface and enable packet delivery. IPv4 uses 32 bits, usually displayed in dotted decimal notation, such as 192.168.1.10. IPv6 uses 128 bits and is writte n in hexadecimal groups separated by colons. A device may have different IP addresses on different networks, and addresses may change when it moves or reconnects. When information is transmitted, it is carried in manageable units. An IP packet contains a h eader and a payload. The header includes information such as the source and destination IP addresses; the payload contains data from higher layers. Routers inspect destination addressing information and use routing tables to choose the next hop. The path i s not necessarily a single direct cable from sender to receiver. Packet switching lets many users share network links. A video, file or webpage can be transported as multiple packets, which may arrive at different times. By contrast, traditional circuit sw itching establishes a reserved communication circuit for a call. Packet switching is efficient for bursty computer data because link capacity is shared rather than permanently reserved for each user. IP itself does not guarantee that packets arrive, arrive once, or arrive in order. The Internet Protocol (IP) supplies logical addresses so data can be delivered between networks. IPv4 addresses contain 32 bits and are commonly written as four decimal numbers, such as 192.168.1.10. IPv6 addresses contain 128 bi ts and are written in hexadecimal groups, providing a much larger address space. Network data is carried in packets with a header containing information such as source and destination addresses and a payload containing data. Routers examine destination inf ormation and forward packets toward the next network. In packet switching, packets can share links with traffic from other users and may follow different paths; the destination system assembles the delivered information as required. In contrast, traditiona l circuit switching reserves a dedicated communication path for the duration of a session.

5 TCP and UDP (Slides 31 – 32) TCP is useful when applications require an ordered, reliable stream of bytes. Before normal data transfer, TCP establishes a connection. I t numbers bytes, receives acknowledgements, retransmits data when necessary, and regulates transmission to avoid overwhelming receivers and networks. For example, a downloaded document must arrive with all its bytes in the correct order; TCP helps provide this behavior. UDP is a simpler transport protocol that sends independent datagrams without first establishing a TCP - style connection. Its header is small, and it does not itself guarantee delivery, ordering or retransmission. This can be useful for live v oice, online games and short queries, where waiting for an old message may be less valuable than receiving a fresh one. Applications can add their own reliability or security mechanisms above UDP when required. An important distinction is that TCP and UDP both use port numbers to identify application processes. IP addresses help find the correct host, while ports help deliver data to the correct service on that host. Neither protocol is automatically secure; security is supplied by additional mechanisms suc h as TLS or application - level protections. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a connection - oriented byte stream. It uses sequence numbers, acknowledgements, retransmissions and flow/congestion control to help applications receive data reliably an d in order. This is valuable for web transfers, files and many email operations. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and has a small header; it sends datagrams without built - in guarantees of delivery, order or retransmission. Applications such a s real - time voice, gaming and DNS often use UDP because low overhead and timely delivery are useful. UDP is not inherently “better” or always faster; the choice depends on application requirements. Application protocols and the complete journey (Slides 33 – 36) When a student types a website address, the browser needs to locate the correct server. DNS (Domain Name System) helps resolve a human - readable domain name to an IP address. The browser then communicates with the server using HTTP or HTTPS. HTTP define s requests and responses; HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS, which helps provide confidentiality, integrity and server authentication. Email uses different application protocols for different jobs. SMTP sends or relays outgoing email. IMAP allows a client to access and synchronize messages held on a mail server, while POP3 is traditionally used to retrieve messages. These protocols perform application - specific tasks but depend on lower layers for moving their data. The complete journey can be traced as follows : application prepares a request; transport adds process - level delivery information; IP adds logical addressing; the local - network technology transmits a frame to the next hop; routers forward the packet through successive networks; the destination process es the layers and passes the request to the server application. The response

6 follows a corresponding path back. Students should practice identifying the role of each layer rather than memorizing only protocol names. HTTP transfers web requests and response s, while HTTPS protects HTTP communication using TLS. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses so applications can locate services. SMTP is used for sending and relaying email, while IMAP and POP3 support retrieval or access to messages. When a studen t enters a website address, the device may first resolve its name using DNS, establish a suitable transport connection, send an HTTP/HTTPS request, and receive a response. The application message is encapsulated in transport data, IP packets and local - netw ork frames; at the destination these layers are processed in reverse. Different links can use different local - network technologies while IP enables the end - to - end journey. 1.2 WIRED & WIRELESS NETWORKING Host - to - network layer and IEEE 802 (Slides 37 – 39) Be fore a device can access the Internet, it must connect to a local network. This first step may use an Ethernet cable, Wi - Fi radio link, or another access technology. The Host - to - Network layer prepares IP packets for the local medium by placing them in fram es and transmitting those frames as signals. The local frame format may change at each network hop even while the IP packet continues toward its destination. IEEE develops technical standards that help equipment from different manufacturers work together. IEEE 802.3 specifies Ethernet technologies; IEEE 802.11 covers wireless LAN technologies; IEEE 802.15 includes wireless personal - area network standards. Standardization matters because a laptop, switch and access point may come from different companies yet still communicate using agreed specifications. A useful distinction is between a switch and a router. A switch typically forwards Ethernet frames within a LAN using local addresses. A router forwards IP packets between different networks. Many home device s combine switching, routing, Wi - Fi access and other functions in a single box. The host - to - network layer connects a computer or IoT device to its immediate network. It includes framing, local delivery and transmission through physical media. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) develops many important local networking standards. The IEEE 802 family includes IEEE 802.3 for Ethernet, IEEE 802.11 for wireless LANs, and IEEE 802.15 standards associated with wireless personal - area networ king. Standardization allows products from different manufacturers to interoperate. Ethernet and wired LANs (Slide 40) Ethernet is a widely used wired LAN technology. A typical laboratory arrangement has several computers connected by twisted - pair copper cables to an Ethernet switch. Each Ethernet network

7 interface has a link - layer address, commonly called a MAC address, used for local delivery. The switch learns which devices are reachable through which ports and forwards frames accordingly. Unshielded tw isted - pair (UTP) cable is affordable and common for desktop connections. Fiber - optic cable carries information using light and is especially useful for high bandwidth, long distances and resistance to electromagnetic interference. Coaxial cable was importa nt in early Ethernet and remains relevant in some other communication systems. Different media have different cost, distance and installation characteristics. Network topology describes how devices are arranged or interconnected. Bus, ring, star, mesh and hybrid are common conceptual topologies. Modern switched Ethernet usually uses a physical star or extended - star arrangement. If a cable between one computer and the switch fails, other computers may continue working, whereas failure of the central switch a ffects its connected devices. Ethernet is widely used to connect devices within offices, laboratories and campuses. Common physical media include unshielded twisted - pair copper cables and optical fiber; coaxial cable has historical and specialized uses. Co pper Ethernet typically connects endpoints to switches; fiber supports long distances and high bandwidth. A star topology with a central switch is common in modern Ethernet LANs. Bus and ring are useful topologies to understand historically or conceptually , but should not be assumed to describe most modern switched Ethernet installations. Ethernet is valued for predictable connectivity and high throughput. Wi - Fi and wireless LANs (Slide 41) Wi - Fi allows devices to connect to a local network using radio wave s. A wireless access point advertises a network and exchanges frames with nearby wireless stations. The access point often connects by Ethernet to the rest of the LAN. In a home, the same physical device may contain the access point, Internet router and sw itch. Wi - Fi commonly operates in 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, with 6 GHz available for supported devices and permitted regions. The 2.4 GHz band often provides better coverage through some obstacles but is frequently crowded. Higher - frequency bands can support wider channels and high throughput but coverage depends on walls, distance and radio conditions. Actual speed varies with interference, device capabilities, channel conditions and number of users. Wireless convenience creates security requirements. A protected Wi - Fi network uses modern security settings such as WPA2 or WPA3 and strong credentials. Students should distinguish Wi - Fi, which provides local wireless access, from the Internet, which is the wider interconnected network that the access point o r router may lead to. A wireless LAN connects nearby devices using radio waves instead of a cable. Wi - Fi implements IEEE 802.11 standards and commonly uses the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands where supported. A wireless access point connects wireless device s to a local network; a home router often combines an access point, switch and Internet gateway. Wi - Fi is used in homes, campuses, hospitals and public spaces. Performance depends on signal strength, interference, channel width, number of

8 users and device capabilities. Security mechanisms such as WPA2 or WPA3 help protect wireless access. WPAN, Bluetooth and Zigbee (Slide 42) A wireless personal - area network covers a small area around a person or set of nearby devices. For example, a phone may communicate w ith wireless earbuds, a smartwatch and a keyboard using Bluetooth. This avoids cables and allows small devices to exchange data at modest power levels. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is especially useful for battery - powered devices that periodically exchange s mall amounts of information. Zigbee is commonly used for low - power sensor and smart - building networks, often with mesh networking in which suitable devices relay messages for others. Zigbee uses IEEE 802.15.4 radio technology but adds higher - level networki ng and application functions. Choose the technology according to the application. Audio accessories commonly use Bluetooth; a room of battery - powered sensors may use BLE or Zigbee; and a laptop downloading large files usually uses Wi - Fi or Ethernet. Range, energy use, data rate, cost and network size are important selection factors. A wireless personal - area network (WPAN) serves a small area around a person or device. Bluetooth is common for headphones, keyboards, wearables and short - range device links. Blu etooth Low Energy (BLE) is designed for applications where low power consumption matters. Zigbee is a low - power networking technology commonly used for sensors and smart - home automation and builds on IEEE 802.15.4 radio technology. Bluetooth and Zigbee dif fer in protocol architecture and application focus; both are useful where small devices need short - range communication. Radio waves and the electromagnetic spectrum (Slide 43) Electromagnetic waves carry energy and information without requiring a physical wire. Their frequency, measured in hertz (Hz), tells us how many oscillations occur each second. Wavelength, measured in meters, is the physical length of one cycle. In free space, their relationship is c = f × λ, where c is approximately 3 × 10^8 meters p er second. For example, a 2.4 GHz radio wave has a free - space wavelength of approximately 0.125 m, or 12.5 cm. As frequency increases, wavelength decreases. Radio - system design depends on more than frequency alone: antennas, transmit power, bandwidth, obst acles, interference and regulations all affect performance. The spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light and higher - frequency radiation. Radio broadcasting, cellular communication, Wi - Fi, point - to - point microwave links and satelli te links occupy different allocated bands. The slides emphasize that wireless communication is possible because electromagnetic waves can carry modulated information between transmitters and receivers.

9 Wireless systems transmit information using electromag netic waves. Radio waves are part of the wider electromagnetic spectrum, which also includes infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X - rays. Frequency is the number of cycles per second; wavelength is the distance between successive wave peaks. Their rela tionship is c = f × λ, where c is the speed of light, f is frequency and λ is wavelength. Frequency influences antenna size, propagation, available bandwidth and penetration. Lower - frequency signals often propagate farther under comparable conditions, whil e higher bands can offer more bandwidth but may be more easily blocked. Different services — broadcast radio, mobile networks, Wi - Fi, microwave links and satellites — use different frequency allocations. Wide - area networking and connecting networks (Slides 44 – 46) A local area network typically serves a room, building or campus; a wide area network (WAN) connects networks over much larger distances. For example, a university may have separate LANs at two campuses and use a service - provider connection to exchange information between them. A WAN is defined by geographic scope and interconnection purpose, not by one specific cable or radio technology. Wired WAN services commonly use optical fiber and provider infrastructure. Wireless WAN approaches include cellular networks, microwave backhaul and satellites. A leased connection offers dedicated connectivity; a virtual private network (VPN) can create an encrypted logical connection over another network, often the public Internet. Each choice involves trade - offs in b andwidth, availability, cost, latency and security. Routers connect these networks and use IP routing to forward traffic. A packet may pass from a phone to a cellular network, through an operator core network, across Internet service providers and finally into a data center. This is why internetworking depends on common protocols even when the underlying transmission technologies differ. A WAN connects networks across cities, regions or countries. Wireless WAN technologies include cellular networks, microwa ve links and satellite communication. Wired WAN connections commonly use optical fiber and service - provider infrastructure. Organizations may use leased links, provider - managed services or encrypted Internet - based VPNs. Routers interconnect LANs, WANs and other networks, forwarding packets toward their destination. A smartphone may connect through cellular service while a laptop uses Wi - Fi, yet both can reach the same Internet service through IP - based internetworking. Client – server request and response (Sli des 47 – 49) The client – server model describes how one application requests a service from another. A web browser is a client, and a website hosted on a server provides pages or other resources. The client sends a request, the server processes it, and the se rver returns a response. A server may support many clients at the same time. In the presentation, a laptop in a VIT laboratory requests a webpage. Its message moves through a switch, campus router, ISP and the Internet before reaching the web server. At ea ch router, the

10 local frame is processed and a new frame is used for the next link. The server returns a response, which is routed back toward the client and displayed by the browser. This example links the entire networking unit: DNS may find the server, H TTP/HTTPS describes the web exchange, TCP or another suitable transport carries application data, IP provides inter - network routing, and Ethernet or Wi - Fi handles local transmission. The same general pattern supports online learning portals, digital paymen ts and many cloud applications. In a client – server system, a client application requests a resource or service and a server processes the request and returns a response. For example, a browser on a campus laptop requests a webpage hosted on a remote server . The request travels through the local switch or access point, campus router, Internet service provider and Internet toward the server. The reply follows a route back to the client; the return path need not be identical. At each network hop, local link - la yer framing can change, while IP addressing enables routing across different networks. The browser then displays the returned content. 1.3 IoT, EDGE/FOG & CLOUD COMPUTING From Internet to Internet of Things (Slides 50 – 53) The Internet of Things (IoT) conne cts physical objects that can sense their environment, exchange data and sometimes perform actions. Examples include smartwatches, smart lights, connected vehicles, industrial machines and automated irrigation systems. An IoT system is not merely an object with Internet access; its usefulness comes from turning physical measurements into information or control. An IoT “thing” usually contains a sensor or another data source, a controller or processor, a communication interface and a power supply. If it cont rols the physical environment, it also has an actuator such as a motor, relay or valve. Some devices connect directly to the Internet, while others communicate through a phone, local gateway or industrial network. The basic IoT cycle is: observe a conditio n, process the measurement, communicate useful data, make a decision and take action or inform a user. The cycle may repeat continuously. This connection between physical systems and digital computing is central to smart agriculture, smart buildings, healt hcare and industrial automation. The Internet initially connected computers and then enabled people to exchange information at global scale. The Internet of Things (IoT) connects physical objects that can sense conditions, process information, communicate and sometimes act. An IoT system may include sensors, an embedded controller, a communication module, a power source and an actuator. Examples include smartwatches, connected vehicles, environmental monitoring stations and irrigation controllers. A connect ed “thing” is useful because it links observations from the physical world with digital decisions and actions.

11 Sensing and embedded processing (Slides 54 – 55) A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical or digital representation. Temperature sensors measure heat conditions, soil - moisture sensors estimate moisture in soil, motion sensors detect movement, and optical sensors respond to light. A sensor alone generally does not understand what a measurement means or decide how a system should resp ond. A controller reads the sensor output and executes instructions. Microcontrollers such as Arduino - compatible boards, ESP32 or STM32 - based systems are common in embedded projects. Single - board computers such as Raspberry Pi can run more complex software and support applications requiring greater computing resources. Industrial programmable logic controllers (PLCs) are designed for reliable automation and control in factories. Consider a temperature sensor attached to an ESP32. The sensor provides a measu rement; the ESP32 converts or reads the value, compares it with a programmed threshold and may send a message using Wi - Fi. If the measured temperature exceeds the safe limit, the controller can activate a fan or send an alert. This shows why sensing and pr ocessing are distinct stages. A sensor converts a physical quantity such as temperature, light, motion, heart rate or soil moisture into an electrical or digital signal. A sensor alone generally cannot provide the complete processing and network functions of an IoT system. A controller or processor reads sensor values, applies logic, prepares messages and controls communication or actuators. Examples shown in the slides include Arduino boards, ESP32, ESP8266, Raspberry Pi, STM32, BBC micro:bit and industria l PLCs. These platforms differ in processing power, interfaces, operating environment and suitability for industrial or educational use. Connecting the device and using the cloud (Slides 56 – 57) Once a controller has useful data, it must select a communicat ion technology. Wi - Fi suits many indoor connected devices; BLE is useful for low - power communication with a nearby phone; Zigbee is used for low - power local networks; cellular links offer wider coverage; Ethernet provides wired connectivity; and LoRa/LoRaW AN can support long - range, low - data - rate sensor applications. Each option has different range, bandwidth, energy and infrastructure needs. A gateway or router often connects local devices to the Internet. For example, a smartwatch may send a measurement to a smartphone over Bluetooth, after which the phone uploads it through Wi - Fi or cellular service. An irrigation controller may use Wi - Fi to reach a router, which passes data through an ISP to a cloud service. The cloud is a collection of remotely accessibl e computing services. It can store readings, create graphs, detect patterns, send notifications and deliver control commands. Cloud computing is valuable for history and large - scale analysis, but basic local control need not wait for a distant cloud if imm ediate action is required. After a controller processes a sensor reading, it can send data through Wi - Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, cellular networks, Ethernet or LoRa/LoRaWAN, depending on range, power, data rate and

12 infrastructure needs. Some devices connect di rectly to a router or gateway; others send data first to a phone or specialized gateway. The Internet can carry this data to cloud services that store historical readings, process information, detect patterns, generate alerts and send control commands. For instance, a wearable may send a heart - rate reading to a phone, which forwards it to a cloud application. Actuation and the smart - irrigation cycle (Slides 58 – 59) An actuator is a component that produces a physical effect after receiving a command. Examples include a relay switching electrical power, a valve controlling water flow, a motor moving a mechanism, or a buzzer producing sound. Sensors observe; processors decide; actuators act. Keeping these functions separate makes the system easier to understand and design. In smart irrigation, a soil - moisture sensor measures moisture. A controller compares the reading with a chosen threshold. If the soil is too dry, it can activate a relay that powers a water pump or opens a valve. When moisture reaches the requi red level, the controller stops watering. A connected version can also send measurements to a dashboard and allow remote supervision. This is a closed - loop control process because the sensor measures the result of the action and the controller adjusts acco rdingly. Practical systems also require safety conditions, such as a maximum pump - on time, protection against running dry, and suitable electrical isolation. The key idea is that IoT produces real - world value when sensed information leads to a meaningful r esponse. IoT systems can inform users through dashboards and alerts or act on the physical world using relays, motors, valves, buzzers and lights. Consider smart irrigation: a soil - moisture sensor measures dryness; an ESP32 or similar controller reads the value and determines whether watering is required. The reading may be transmitted to a cloud service for monitoring, while a decision can be made locally or remotely. A command operates a relay or motor controller, starting the water pump or opening a valv e. As the soil becomes sufficiently moist, the system stops watering and continues sensing. This repeated sense – process – connect – decide – act cycle is called closed - loop monitoring and control. Why not send everything to the cloud? (Slides 60 – 62) Sending all raw data to a distant cloud can be convenient, but it may create delays, consume network bandwidth and increase storage and processing costs. Continuous video from many cameras, for example, generates much more data than occasional temperature readings. Tr ansmitting everything is not always necessary if the application only needs a small event or summary. Cloud dependence also raises reliability concerns. A connected irrigation controller should ideally maintain essential local operation even if Internet co nnectivity is interrupted. Privacy and security matter because raw sensor streams may reveal personal activity or sensitive operational information. These factors motivate processing data nearer to its source.

13 Local processing might mean checking a tempera ture threshold on the microcontroller, detecting a vehicle in a camera feed using a nearby computer, or filtering repeated sensor readings before upload. The cloud can still receive important events, periodic summaries and historical data. This division of work leads to edge and fog computing. Sending all raw sensor data to distant cloud servers is simple in concept, but may cause high network traffic, additional costs, delays, dependence on Internet availability and privacy risks. For example, an ambulance - detection camera or industrial safety sensor may need a decision immediately. Processing data at or near the device reduces response time and allows only useful results or summaries to be uploaded. Local processing does not eliminate the cloud; it complem ents cloud storage and advanced analysis. Edge, fog and cloud computing (Slides 63 – 66) Edge computing processes data at or very close to the source. A smart camera that detects movement locally is an edge device. Fog computing places additional processing and coordination within a nearby local network, such as a gateway or local server managing several cameras. Cloud computing provides centralized or remote resources for large - scale storage, advanced analytics and services accessible from many locations. Th e difference is primarily where computation occurs and what job it performs. Edge devices can respond quickly and reduce raw data transmission. Fog nodes can combine data from multiple nearby devices and coordinate local actions. Cloud systems can train co mplex models, retain long histories and analyze patterns across a city or organization. The ambulance - priority example illustrates all three. A roadside camera and edge computer recognize an approaching ambulance and trigger an immediate signal change. A f og controller coordinates upcoming junctions to create a green corridor. A cloud service stores event data, informs stakeholders and studies longer - term traffic patterns. Actual systems require reliable detection, traffic - safety logic and appropriate autho rity; the example is a conceptual architecture. Edge computing processes data on or very close to the device, such as an embedded board, camera or local industrial computer. Fog computing places computation in nearby network infrastructure, such as a local gateway or area server that coordinates several devices. Cloud computing uses remote data centers for large - scale storage, analytics, model training and shared services. In the smart - traffic example, an edge camera detects an ambulance and can trigger an immediate local response; a fog controller coordinates signals at nearby junctions; the cloud aggregates information for city - level analysis and planning. The boundaries between edge and fog can vary by architecture, but the key distinction is where proces sing takes place. What the cloud and data centers contain (Slides 67 – 69) The cloud is not an invisible computer floating in the sky. It runs on real infrastructure in data centers: racks of servers, storage equipment, networking switches and routers, power systems and

14 cooling facilities. These resources are managed so users can access applications and data through the Internet without owning all the physical hardware themselves. Cloud storage keeps information such as documents, images, videos, sensor logs and databases. Cloud computation uses processors to execute applications, analyze data and run AI models. The two functions are complementary: a stored video is simply data until an application processes it, for example to detect vehicles or produce a summ ary. Cloud services can scale resources according to demand, support remote collaboration and provide backups and redundancy. However, they still depend on connectivity, security controls and responsible data management. Examples familiar to students inclu de online file storage, streaming platforms, email and web - based applications. The cloud is not simply an abstract symbol: it consists of remote computing, storage and networking resources delivered over networks. Data centers contain server racks, process ors, storage systems, network switches and routers, cooling systems, backup power and physical security. Cloud storage keeps files, databases, videos and backups, while cloud computation executes applications, analysis and AI workloads. An application may store uploaded video in cloud storage and later use cloud processors to analyze its content. Storage preserves data; computation performs work on that data. Sequential, parallel, CPU and GPU computing (Slides 70 – 73) Sequential processing performs one operation or task after another. Parallel processing divides suitable work into pieces that can run simultaneously on multiple processing units. A restaurant analogy helps: one chef preparing four dishes in sequence may t ake longer than four chefs preparing different dishes at the same time. Parallel processing helps only when the work can be divided and coordinated effectively. A CPU (Central Processing Unit) is a general - purpose processor designed to handle a wide variet y of tasks, including operating - system functions, application logic and control decisions. A GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) contains many processing units optimized for executing large numbers of similar calculations in parallel. GPUs are useful for graphi cs rendering, image processing, scientific computation and many AI workloads. AI systems often involve matrix and tensor calculations repeated across large datasets. GPUs can accelerate these calculations because many operations can be performed concurrent ly. However, a GPU does not automatically outperform a CPU on every task. Small, sequential or control - heavy tasks may run more efficiently on a CPU. Modern systems frequently use both, assigning each processor the work it handles best. Sequential processi ng executes operations one after another. Parallel processing divides suitable work into parts that can execute simultaneously on multiple processing units. A CPU (Central Processing Unit) is a general - purpose processor designed to handle diverse tasks and control complex program execution. A GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) contains many processing units optimized for highly parallel operations, such as graphics and large numerical computations. AI

15 training and inference often involve repeated matrix calcula tions that benefit from GPUs. However, not every problem can be parallelized, and actual performance depends on data movement, algorithms and hardware. From computing to mobile connectivity (Slides 74 – 75) Computing creates useful information, but connected applications must also exchange it while users or machines move. A car cannot depend only on a fixed cable, and a doctor providing remote consultation needs communication with a patient who may be far away. Mobile communication enables connectivity across changing locations through wireless infrastructure. Examples include connected vehicles reporting conditions, wearables sending health measurements, smart - city sensors communicating with control centers, and smartphones supporting video calls and cloud ap plications. These applications demand different combinations of coverage, speed, reliability and response time. The transition from computing to mobile communication therefore asks a new question: how can many moving devices remain connected reliably? The evolution from 1G through 5G provides the technological background for this capability. Powerful computation becomes more useful when devices can communicate continuously while moving. Connected vehicles, remote healthcare, smart infrastructure and mobile applications need communication networks with broad coverage, sufficient capacity and acceptable response times. This requirement leads naturally to the evolution of mobile communication technologies. 1.4 MOBILE COMMUNICATION: 1G TO 5G & BEYOND Evolution o f mobile generations (Slide 76) First - generation (1G) cellular systems introduced analog mobile voice communication. Second - generation (2G) systems moved to digital voice and popularized SMS. Third - generation (3G) expanded mobile data capabilities and made Internet access more practical. Fourth - generation (4G), especially LTE, enabled much faster packet - based mobile broadband, supporting video streaming, apps and cloud services. Fifth - generation (5G) networks extend mobile connectivity toward higher capacit y, lower latency in suitable deployments and support for large numbers of connected devices. Each generation builds on advances in radio technology, network architecture, devices and spectrum usage. Actual user experience depends on network coverage, spect rum, deployment and device support. Think of the evolution as a shift in primary emphasis: 1G focused on mobile voice; 2G digitized voice and messaging; 3G expanded mobile Internet; 4G supported broadband applications; and 5G is designed for a broader mix of people, machines and time - sensitive services. First - generation (1G) mobile systems supported analog voice calls. Second - generation (2G) systems introduced digital voice and SMS. Third - generation (3G) systems made mobile Internet and

16 multimedia services more practical. Fourth - generation (4G), particularly LTE, provided high - speed packet - based mobile broadband and enabled widespread video streaming, apps and cloud services. Fifth - generation (5G) extends capacity and supports new requirements including low latency and large numbers of connected devices. The generations represent broad changes in network capability, not a guarantee that every device or operator provides every advertised feature. Key features of 5G (Slide 77) 5G is often explained using three broad capabilities. Enhanced mobile broadband supports high data rates and network capacity. Ultra - reliable low - latency communication targets demanding applications that require timely and dependable responses. Massive machine - type communication addresses large numbers of connected sensors and devices sending relatively small amounts of data. Latency means the time taken for data to travel and a response to return or for a network operation to complete, depending on the measurement. Lower latency is importa nt for some control and interactive applications. However, the extremely low values sometimes quoted for 5G are design targets under particular conditions, not guaranteed end - to - end times for every user or application. For example, a high - resolution video stream emphasizes throughput, a remote - control system emphasizes latency and reliability, and a large sensor network emphasizes device density and energy efficiency. These requirements differ, so one network must support multiple service profiles. 5G is de signed around enhanced mobile broadband (high data rates), ultra - reliable low - latency communication for suitable deployments, and massive machine - type communication for large numbers of devices. High speed supports demanding applications, low latency helps time - sensitive communication, and high connection density supports IoT systems. Actual speed, latency and capacity depend on spectrum, network deployment, device capability, congestion and application architecture; figures on slides are illustrative rathe r than guaranteed everyday performance. 5G applications and emerging 6G (Slides 78 – 79) Connected and autonomous vehicles can exchange traffic information and receive map or infrastructure updates. Remote healthcare can support video consultations, monitori ng and transmission of medical information. Smart factories can connect machines, robots and monitoring systems. Smart cities may use connectivity for traffic, utilities and environmental sensing. 5G can support these applications, although safe deployment also depends on sensors, software, regulation and system engineering. 6G is a research and future - standardization direction rather than a universally deployed commercial network today. Proposed goals include further advances in capacity, latency, sensing, AI - assisted networking, energy efficiency and integration of terrestrial and non - terrestrial communication. Specific performance figures and applications are aspirations and should not be treated as guaranteed capabilities.

17 The key lesson is that new mobi le generations do more than increase download speed. They enable new ways of connecting people, devices, industries and services, while also increasing the importance of trustworthy operation and cybersecurity. Potential and growing 5G applications include connected vehicles, remote patient monitoring, smart factories, industrial sensors, robotics and smart - city infrastructure. Some demanding applications require additional edge computing, dependable coverage and safety mechanisms beyond the radio network i tself. Sixth - generation (6G) is a future research and standardization direction, often associated with AI - native networking, sensing, immersive experiences, sustainability and tighter integration of communication and computation. Its capabilities and deplo yment timelines remain prospective rather than established universal services. 1.5 CYBERSECURITY IN THE CONNECTED WORLD Why cybersecurity matters (Slides 80 – 81) As more devices, accounts and services become connected, more information and functions become reachable through networks. A smartphone may contain academic records, personal photographs, payment apps and authentication messages. A connected machine may control a physical process. Cybersecurity protects these devices, networks, data and users from u nauthorized access, misuse, damage and disruption. Security is not limited to preventing hackers from stealing passwords. It also includes preventing unauthorized changes to records, maintaining service availability, protecting privacy and recovering after incidents. A secure system needs a combination of technical safeguards, organizational procedures and responsible user behavior. Consider an online student portal. Students should see only their own records; marks should not be changed without authorizati on; and the portal should remain available during important academic activities. These three needs lead to the CIA triad. As more devices, people and services become connected, more information is exposed to potential misuse. Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting devices, networks, data and digital identities against unauthorized access, damage, theft and disruption. A secure system needs both technical controls and responsible user behavior. Security matters for student portals, banking, smart homes, industrial systems and connected healthcare. Confidentiality, integrity and availability (Slide 82) Confidentiality means information is accessible only to authorized people or systems. Examples include restricting access to student marks, bank details an d private messages. Passwords, access permissions and encryption help support confidentiality. Confidentiality does not mean hiding all data from everyone; it means allowing access according to legitimate roles.

18 Integrity means data remains accurate and is not modified improperly. A marksheet must not be altered by an unauthorized person. Checksums, digital signatures, audit trails and controlled permissions can help detect or prevent unauthorized changes. Availability means systems and data remain accessib le when legitimate users need them. Backups, redundancy, monitoring and maintenance support availability. The three goals can interact. A website that is highly available but leaks private data is not secure. A perfectly confidential database that cannot be accessed when needed is also inadequate. Cybersecurity requires balancing confidentiality, integrity and availability according to the application. The CIA triad summarizes three central security objectives. Confidentiality means information is accessib le only to authorized people; student marks and banking records should not be visible to strangers. Integrity means information remains accurate and is not changed without authorization; grades and transactions must not be secretly modified. Availability m eans authorized users can access systems and data when required; an online examination or learning portal must remain usable. Effective security balances all three goals. Vulnerabilities, threats and attacks (Slide 83) A vulnerability is a weakness that co uld be exploited, such as an easy - to - guess password, outdated software or an incorrectly configured service. A threat is a potential source of harm, such as a criminal attacker, malicious program or accidental misuse. An attack is an attempt to exploit a w eakness, and the impact is the resulting loss or disruption. For example, a student uses the password “123456.” An attacker attempts common passwords and successfully signs in. The vulnerability was the weak password, the threat was the attacker, the attac k was unauthorized login, and the impact could be exposure or misuse of the student’s data. This chain explains why small weaknesses can have serious consequences. Risk can be reduced by removing vulnerabilities, limiting privileges, monitoring activity an d preparing recovery measures. No single control eliminates all cyber risk, so practical security uses multiple protective layers. A vulnerability is a weakness, such as a simple password or outdated software. A threat is a person, event or condition that could exploit a weakness. An attack is an attempt to exploit the vulnerability, and the impact may include data theft, financial loss or service disruption. For example, a weak password may allow an attacker to guess credentials and gain unauthorized acces s. Reducing vulnerabilities lowers the opportunity for successful attacks. Encryption and where it is used (Slides 84 – 85) Encryption transforms readable information, called plaintext, into an unreadable form, called ciphertext, using an algorithm and a key . An authorized party with the appropriate key can decrypt

19 it. Encryption helps protect confidentiality when information travels across networks or is stored on devices and servers. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret key for encryption and decryptio n. Asymmetric encryption uses a related public/private key pair for specific cryptographic operations, including secure key establishment and digital signatures. Real secure communication systems often combine these approaches. Encryption is not the same a s authentication: encrypted data can be private, but the system must also establish who is communicating. Examples include HTTPS connections to websites, encrypted messaging, secure Wi - Fi and encryption of files stored on a device or cloud service. Data in transit means information moving between systems; data at rest means information stored on a disk or other medium. Both can need protection. Encryption is effective only when keys and endpoints are also protected. Encryption transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key. Decryption restores readable information for an authorized party with the appropriate key. Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key for encryption and decryption; asymmetric cryptography uses a related pub lic and private key pair. In practice, secure protocols such as HTTPS/TLS combine cryptographic techniques. Encryption helps protect data in transit over networks and data at rest on devices or servers. It does not by itself prevent every attack: key prote ction, authentication and secure software are also essential. Authentication and multi - factor security (Slide 86) Authentication is the process of verifying an identity. A password or PIN is something a user knows; a phone, hardware security key or one - tim e code can represent something the user has; and a fingerprint or face scan relates to something the user is. These are commonly described as authentication - factor categories. Multi - factor authentication (MFA) combines factors from different categories, ma king account takeover harder if one factor is compromised. For example, signing in with a password and then approving a request on a registered device is stronger than using a password alone. Two passwords do not constitute two different factors. Authentic ation should be distinguished from authorization. Authentication answers “Who are you?” Authorization answers “What are you allowed to access?” After a student logs in, the portal must still restrict access to that student’s permitted information. Users sh ould never share OTPs or approve unexpected sign - in requests. Authentication verifies that a user or device is who it claims to be. Factors may be something you know (password or PIN), something you have (phone, security key or authenticator), or something you are (fingerprint or face). Multi - factor authentication (MFA) combines different factors, reducing the risk that a stolen password alone will grant access. Authorization is different: after identity is verified, authorization determines what resources that user may access.

20 Passwords, phishing and social engineering (Slides 87 – 89) A strong password is long, unique and difficult to predict. A passphrase made from several unrelated words can be easier to remember than a short complicated string. Password r euse is risky because a breach at one service can expose accounts at other services. Password managers can help generate and store unique credentials, and MFA adds protection. Phishing is an attempt to trick a person into revealing information or taking an unsafe action, often through a fraudulent email, text message or website. Warning signs include unexpected urgency, suspicious links, requests for passwords or OTPs, and claims that an account will be blocked immediately. Attackers may copy the appearance of legitimate organizations. Social engineering is the broader manipulation of human trust. It can involve fake technical - support calls, impersonation of a supervisor, attractive offers or fraudulent requests for confidential information. The safest respo nse is to verify through a known official channel rather than through contact details supplied in the suspicious message. A strong password should be long, unique for each account and difficult to guess. A password manager can help generate and store uniqu e credentials. Phishing uses fraudulent messages, websites or links to trick people into revealing credentials, payment details or OTPs, or into installing malware. Social engineering is the broader manipulation of human trust through impersonation, urgenc y, fear or attractive offers. Never share OTPs or passwords, and verify suspicious requests through a trusted channel rather than the contact information supplied in the message. Malware and ransomware (Slides 90 – 91) Malware is software created to perform harmful or unauthorized actions. A computer virus attaches to other files or programs and spreads when infected content is executed. A worm can propagate across systems or networks without requiring the same type of host - file attachment. A Trojan appears t o be legitimate software while concealing malicious behavior. Spyware secretly collects information about users or systems. Ransomware is a form of malware that may encrypt files or otherwise block access and demand payment. It can interrupt teaching, hosp ital services, business operations and personal access to important documents. Paying a ransom does not guarantee recovery, and attackers may also threaten to disclose stolen information. Risk reduction includes installing software from trusted sources, up dating operating systems and applications, limiting unnecessary permissions, avoiding suspicious attachments and keeping recoverable backups. Backups should be protected and periodically tested, because connected backup storage can sometimes be affected by the same incident. Malware is software designed to damage, disrupt, spy on or gain unauthorized access to systems. A virus attaches to files or programs; a worm can spread through networks; a Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software; and spyware sec retly collects information. Ransomware is malware that locks

21 or encrypts files and demands payment for restoration. Backups, security updates, careful downloads, limited permissions and endpoint protection reduce risk. Paying a ransom does not guarantee re covery. Daily cyber hygiene and unit recap (Slides 92 – 93) Cyber hygiene means adopting routine habits that reduce digital risk. Use strong unique passwords, enable MFA, keep devices updated, lock screens, review permissions and avoid suspicious downloads. Use trusted networks for sensitive tasks and verify the address of a website before entering credentials. Maintain backups of important academic and personal work. When something suspicious happens, do not ignore it. Stop interacting with the suspicious me ssage, avoid sharing further information, change affected credentials through the official service if appropriate, and report the issue to the relevant IT or security team. Prompt reporting can limit damage and protect other users. The complete unit follow s a logical progression. Networks connect devices; protocols enable communication; IoT adds sensing and action; edge, fog and cloud provide computing resources; mobile networks extend connectivity; and cybersecurity protects the entire connected environmen t. Understanding how these ideas work together is more important than memorizing isolated definitions. Cyber hygiene means maintaining safe digital habits: use unique strong passwords, enable MFA, update software, avoid unknown links and attachments, conne ct through trusted networks and back up important files. The entire unit follows a connected story: networks connect devices; protocols allow communication; IoT senses the physical world; edge, fog and cloud systems process information; mobile networks ext end connectivity; and cybersecurity protects the resulting digital environment. The goal is not connectivity alone, but a connected world that is useful, reliable and safe.

What is the Internet of Things (IoT)? IoT is a network of physical objects (“things”) embedded with sensors, software and connectivity, enabling them to collect, exchange and act on data over the Internet. 1 PHYSICAL THING Smartwatch Car • Machine 2 SENSE Sensors collect data 3 CONNECT Wi-Fi • Bluetooth Zigbee • Cellular 4 INTERNET / CLOUD Data is shared & processed 5 ACT Monitor • Alert Control • Automate Example: Smartwatch senses heart rate sends data app/cloud processes it user receives useful information→ → → → IoT = Things + Sensors + Connectivity + Data + Intelligent Action

SENSOR Observes the physical world CONTROLLER Processes data & instructions CONNECTIVITY Communicates with network POWER Battery or electrical supply ACTUATOR Performs a physical action Not every object is an IoT “Thing” — it must be able to sense/act, process and communicate data. Physical Thing = Real-World Object + Embedded Electronics + Connectivity

Stage 2 — SENSE: Sensors Collect Data Sensors detect physical conditions and convert them into data that an IoT system can process. PHYSICAL WORLD Temperature Motion • Light SENSOR Detects / measures a physical quantity DATA Electrical / Digital signal CONTROLLER Reads & processes the data Temperature Smart AC Heart Rate Smartwatch Light Auto Lights Motion Security Moisture Irrigation GPS Vehicle Example: Heartbeat → Heart-rate Sensor → Digital Data → Smartwatch Controller Sensors are the “eyes and ears” of an IoT system.

Stage 5 — INTERNET & CLOUD: Where Does the IoT Data Go? The Internet carries IoT data to cloud platforms, where it can be stored, processed, analyzed and used by applications.
